CVE-2026-106096.title: Cri-o: cri-o: writable linklogs bind mount allows pods to redirect privileged conmon log writes
CVE-2026-106096.description: A flaw was found in CRI-O. When the optional Linux LinkLogs feature is enabled, the host pod log directory is bind-mounted into a pod emptyDir and is intended to be read-only, but Linux ignores MS_RDONLY on the initial bind and the CRI mount stays writable. A non-privileged UID 0 container can place a symlink at a future kubelet log path so that privileged conmon later appends attacker-controlled log data to an existing host file. This is an append-only host integrity issue, not universal remote code execution; LinkLogs is not enabled by default.

CVE-2026-113443.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference in visualTicket
CVE-2026-113443.description:
visualTicket is vulnerable to Insecure Direct Object Reference in the cart service. The server modifies or deletes a cart item based solely on the supplied "cart_id" without checking whether the object belongs to the current symfony session. Cart identifiers are created sequentially and allows prediction of valid values. An attacker holding an independent session can reference another user's "cart_id" and change its state, for example altering the quantity or deleting the item. This issue was fixed in version 20260817.

CVE-2026-126348.title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts with invalid Punycode A-labels
CVE-2026-126348.description: Addressable is an alternative implementation to the URI implementation that is part of Ruby's standard library. From 2.0.0 until 2.9.1, the pure-Ruby Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode implementation decodes invalid Punycode A-labels instead of returning them unchanged. Labels that decode to ASCII text or fail to convert back to the same A-label can therefore make Addressable::URI#display_uri show a trusted-looking host while host, normalized_host, and the connection target retain the attacker-controlled encoded host. A trusted-name comparison using Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode output can also treat two different hosts as the same without displaying the URI. The native libidn implementation, to_ascii, and normalized_host are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 2.9.1.

CVE-2026-135393.title: Pion DTLS: Repeated client certificate verification allows excessive CPU consumption during DTLS handshakes
CVE-2026-135393.description: Pion DTLS is a Go implementation of Datagram Transport Layer Security. From 1.2.2 until 3.1.13, the server state machine did not distinguish successful processing of the client certificate flight from completion of the handshake, so later traffic could revisit the same cached Certificate, ClientKeyExchange, and CertificateVerify messages. A malicious client can withhold Finished and send additional handshake traffic. Depending on the configured authentication policy, repeated work can include certificate parsing, handshake signature verification, and certificate-chain verification. The vulnerable endpoint must act as the DTLS server. Pion WebRTC applications are affected when they operate in that role. Repeated or concurrent attempts can consume excessive CPU resources, delay legitimate connections, and reduce service availability. The issue is fixed in version 3.1.13.

can: raw: add locking for raw flags bitfield

CVE-2026-99376.title: NFSv4/pnfs: Free the netid when draining a data-server address list
CVE-2026-99376.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

NFSv4/pnfs: Free the netid when draining a data-server address list

nfs4_pnfs_ds_addr_free() releases all three of an address entry's
allocations, but the four sites that drain a decoded list before it
reaches a data server open-code the loop and free only da_remotestr and
the entry, leaking da_netid. Both layout drivers drain that list when
nfs4_pnfs_ds_add() returned a data server already in the cache, and
again on their error exits.

Lift the drain into nfs4_pnfs_ds_addr_list_free() so an address list has
one owner. A striping mount reaches the cached case on nearly every
GETDEVICEINFO, since many deviceIDs name the same data servers.
